paragraphs: **Rabbi Tarfon (the priest).**

This eminent man was called “the father of all Israel” by later generations, as in Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, chapter 1, at the end of halakhah 1, and Yevamot, chapter 4, at the end of halakhah 12. He was exceedingly wealthy and exceptionally tall for his generation. Thus [Niddah 24b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.24b) relates: “Abba Shaul was tall for his generation, and Rabbi Tarfon reached his shoulder. Rabbi Tarfon was tall for his generation, and Rabbi Meir reached his shoulder.” We do not know who this remarkable man’s forebears were. It is, however, quite certain that he was a priest, that his mother too was a priest’s daughter, and that he saw the Temple while it still stood. In [Kiddushin 71a](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.71a), Rabbi Tarfon says: “Once I went up to the platform behind my mother’s brother, and inclined my ear toward the High Priest…”.[^1]

In Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, chapter 1, at the end of halakhah 1, Rabbi Akiva says that only priests without physical blemishes may sound the trumpets. Rabbi Tarfon replies: “May I lose my sons if I did not see my mother’s brother, who was lame in one leg, standing in the Temple courtyard, trumpet in hand, and sounding it!” Rabbi Akiva says: “My master, perhaps you saw this only at the Hakhel assembly?” Rabbi Tarfon acknowledges that this was indeed so, but that he had forgotten the circumstances. In Tosefta Sotah 7:8, instead of “on the day of Hakhel,” the wording is “on that very day,” meaning the day of Hakhel. In [Sifrei Bamidbar, Beha’alotekha, section 75](https://www.sefaria.org/Sifrei_Bamidbar.75), Rabbi Akiva says: “Perhaps it was on Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, or the Jubilee?” *Meir Ayin* has already observed there that the text should read: “Perhaps it was at Hakhel, or on Yom Kippur in the Jubilee year.”[^2]

According to the tradition preserved in *Seder Olam Rabbah*, the Temple was destroyed in the year following a sabbatical year. The Hakhel day mentioned by Rabbi Tarfon must therefore have been at least seven years before the destruction: surely one cannot suppose that Hakhel took place amid the siege and distress! When he witnessed what he later testified to having seen, he was undoubtedly about thirteen years old, since a minor cannot give testimony. He would consequently have been about twenty when the Temple was destroyed. It is therefore very likely that he was a disciple of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, even though he is not counted among that master’s disciples in [Avot 2:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.2.8). That passage lists only the five greatest disciples, who attained authority to issue rulings during their teacher’s lifetime; Rabbi Tarfon was still a young man when Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai died. Moreover, at the end of Tosefta Chagigah, chapter 3, we find Rabbi Tarfon saying: “May I lose my sons if I do not possess this ruling from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.”[^3]

Maimonides, in his introduction to Zeraim, places him in the second group after the destruction, because he was young at the time of the destruction and his active career belongs to the generation of Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues.
Rabbi Tarfon is mentioned forty-nine times in the Mishnah: nine times in Zeraim, six in Moed, nine in Nashim, six in Nezikin, ten in Kodashim, and nine in Tohorot.

His usual disputant is Rabbi Akiva, his disciple-colleague: [Terumot 9:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Terumot.9.2); [Maasrot 3:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Maasrot.3.9); [Maaser Sheni 2:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Maaser_Sheni.2.9), repeated in [Eduyot 1:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eduyot.1.10); [Pesachim 10:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Pesachim.10.6); [Yevamot 15:6–7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yevamot.15.6-7); [Ketubot 5:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Ketubot.5.2) and [9:2–3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Ketubot.9.2-3); [Nazir 6:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Nazir.6.6); [Bava Metzia 2:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.2.7); [Menachot 12:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Menachot.12.5); [Bekhorot 2:6–9](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bekhorot.2.6-9); [Keritot 5:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Keritot.5.2); [Kelim 25:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.25.7); [Oholot 13:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Oholot.13.3) and [16:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Oholot.16.1); and [Makhshirin 5:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Makhshirin.5.4).

He disputes with the Sages in [Kilayim 5:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kilayim.5.8), [Maaser Sheni 2:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Maaser_Sheni.2.4), [Shabbat 2:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Shabbat.2.2), [Bava Kamma 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Kamma.2.5), [Zevachim 11:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Zevachim.11.7), and [Kelim 11:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.11.7). Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Eliezer dispute at the end of [Kiddushin, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kiddushin.3.13). Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira dispute in [Peah 3:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Peah.3.6). He disputes with Rabbi Yehoshua in [Kelim 11:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.11.4). Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Akiva give their opinions in [Terumot 4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Terumot.4.5); Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Tarfon dispute in [Sukkah 3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Sukkah.3.4). Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah and Rabbi Yehoshua call him “Tarfon, my brother” in [Yadayim 4:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yadayim.4.3).

Among his well-known rulings in the Mishnah is [Berakhot 1:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.1.3): “Rabbi Tarfon said: I was once traveling on the road, and reclined to recite the Shema in accordance with the opinion of Beit Shammai, thereby endangering myself because of robbers.” In [Yevamot 15a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.15a), Rabbi Tarfon says: “I long for the time when the case of a daughter’s co-wife will come before me, so that I may marry her.” This does not mean that he was a disciple of Beit Shammai: Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit 4:2, says that he followed Beit Shammai only in these two matters.[^4]

In [Berakhot 6:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.6.8), Rabbi Tarfon gives the blessing “Who creates many living beings.” In [Maaser Sheni 2:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Maaser_Sheni.2.4), he rules that second-tithe vetches which have become impure should be apportioned among batches of dough, since consecrated produce may not be redeemed in order to feed it to dogs. In [Shabbat 2:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Shabbat.2.2), lamps may be lit only with olive oil. In [Pesachim 10:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Pesachim.10.6), one must say: “Who redeemed us and redeemed our ancestors.” In [Yevamot 15:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yevamot.15.7), someone who robbed one of five people places the stolen property among them and withdraws.[^5]

In [Ketubot 5:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Ketubot.5.2), when the appointed time for marriage has arrived but the couple has not married, Rabbi Tarfon says that the woman may receive her entire maintenance in terumah. In [Ketubot 7:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Ketubot.7.6), he adds “a loud-voiced woman” to those who are divorced without receiving their ketubah. In [Ketubot 9:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Ketubot.9.2), the assets are to be given “to the weakest among them.” In [Nazir 5:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Nazir.5.5), none of the people concerned becomes a nazirite, since a nazirite vow requires an explicit, definite declaration. At the end of [Kiddushin, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kiddushin.3.13), mamzerim can arrange for their descendants to acquire an unblemished status. In [Bava Kamma 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Kamma.2.5), an ox which causes damage on the injured party’s property pays full damages. In [Bava Metzia 2:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.2.7), one may use the money obtained from a lost article; and in [Bava Metzia 4:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.4.3), Rabbi Tarfon rules for the merchants of Lod that the threshold for overreaching is one third of the purchase price.[^6]

The familiar designation *palges* for a sheep in its thirteenth month comes from Rabbi Tarfon: [Parah 1:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Parah.1.3). A bolt with a knob at its head is like any other utensil: [Kelim 11:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.11.4). On this basis [Shabbat 124a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.124a) explains that he regards the area within the doorway as outside it.

His rulings in baraitot appear in [Shabbat 139a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.139a), [Pesachim 118a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.118a), [Rosh Hashanah 26a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.26a), [Sukkah 32b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.32b) and [34b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.34b), [Yevamot 122b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.122b), and [Gittin 88b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.88b).

Rabbi Tarfon took a prominent part in the Sanhedrin of Yavneh under Rabban Gamliel’s presidency. Thus [Pesachim 72b](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.72b) relates that Rabbi Tarfon did not come to the study house one evening. In the morning Rabban Gamliel found him and asked why he had not come. “I performed the Temple service,” he replied. Rabban Gamliel asked: “Where is there Temple service nowadays?” Rabbi Tarfon answered: “I ate terumah…”.[^7] Likewise, in [Zevachim 57a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.57a), “This question was asked of the Sages in the vineyard at Yavneh”—and Rabbi Tarfon answered. In Mekhilta, Beshallach, tractate Vayassa, Rabbi Tarfon and the elders sit in the shade of a dovecote at Yavneh.

He was also at Yavneh when Rabban Gamliel was removed from the presidency. Although he is not mentioned in the account in [Berakhot 28a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.28a), he is mentioned in [Yadayim 4:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yadayim.4.3): “On that day they said: What is the law concerning Ammon and Moab in the sabbatical year?” Rabbi Tarfon ruled that the poor tithe should be given, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah ruled that the second tithe should be given. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says: “Yishmael, my brother, I have not changed the established practice—Tarfon, my brother, has changed it.” Rabbi Yehoshua says: “I shall respond to Tarfon, my brother.” It is well known that whenever “on that day” is used, it refers to the day when Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah was appointed president, as in Berakhot 28a.

Why, when they considered whom to appoint in Rabban Gamliel’s place, did they not mention Rabbi Tarfon, though he too was a priest, very wealthy, elderly, and one of the great men of the generation? A very likely explanation is that he was exacting and habitually said “May I lose my sons”: [Oholot 16:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Oholot.16.1); [Shabbat 17a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.17a)—where Rashi explains that he was distressed by Torah being forgotten and cursed himself—and [116a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.116a); [Zevachim 13a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.13a); Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, chapter 1, at the end of halakhah 1; the end of Tosefta Chagigah, chapter 3; and Sifrei, Beha’alotekha, section 37. If he did not spare his own sons’ lives, they were consequently afraid to appoint him president.[^8]

Another possibility is suggested by Kallah Rabbati’s account that he was not particularly generous. The praise given to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah is that he was wealthy: if someone had to attend to the imperial court, he could go and do so.[^9]

Rabbi Tarfon was regularly among the first to speak. In [Kiddushin 40b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.40b), Rabbi Tarfon and the elders are reclining together, and he responds: “Action is greater.” In [Moed Katan 28b](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.28b), when Rabbi Yishmael’s sons died, four elders came to console him—Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yossi HaGelili, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, and Rabbi Akiva—and Rabbi Tarfon was the first to speak. Likewise, in [Sanhedrin 101a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.101a), four elders visit Rabbi Eliezer when he is ill, and Rabbi Tarfon speaks first. In [Gittin 83a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.83a), after Rabbi Eliezer’s death, Rabbi Tarfon is the first to respond. In [Yoma 76a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.76a), he is again named first: Rabbi Elazar HaModai calls him “my master,” while Rabbi Tarfon calls the other “Modai.” In the matter of a daughter’s co-wife, he went with Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, and Rabbi Akiva to Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, as explicitly stated at the end of Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, chapter 1. Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas applied a verse to him as he did to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. Only in the Haggadah’s account of the gathering of Rabbi Eliezer and the others at Bnei Brak is Rabbi Tarfon named last.

His permanent home, however, was Lod in southern Judea, where he was the leading authority. In [Bava Metzia 4:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.4.3), “Rabbi Tarfon ruled in Lod.” In [Chagigah 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.18a), when Aleksa died in Lod and all Israel came to eulogize him, Rabbi Tarfon did not permit them to do so. In [Kiddushin 40b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.40b), he and the elders recline in the upper room of the house of Nitza in Lod. In [Megillah 20a](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.20a), Rabbi Yehuda says: “I was a child, and I read the Megillah before Rabbi Tarfon and the elders in Lod.” In [Taanit 3:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Taanit.3.9), a fast was decreed in Lod, and rain fell before midday. Rabbi Tarfon said: “Go out, eat, and celebrate a festival.”

From this, *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, page 105, conjectures that Rabbi Tarfon established his academy there after Rabbi Eliezer’s death, since Rabbi Eliezer had been in Lod. This is incorrect, as shown by Rabbi Yehuda’s testimony that he read the Megillah before Rabbi Tarfon in Lod when he was a child. We see from this that Rabbi Tarfon was there all along, since Rabbi Yehuda was their outstanding disciple throughout their lives; and Rabbi Eliezer is known to have died after Rabban Gamliel.

The sounder conjecture is that Rabbi Tarfon always lived in Lod. Rabbi Eliezer’s academy was there too, but the Sages are known to have agreed not to enter into scholarly debate with Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Tarfon was undoubtedly included among them. When they visited Rabbi Eliezer in his illness, Rabbi Tarfon was present, as in [Sanhedrin 101a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.101a). Although Rabbi Eliezer had established his academy there, he did not involve himself in the town’s affairs: Rabbi Tarfon was its head, and would occasionally travel to Yavneh. Similarly, Rabbi Akiva’s permanent academy was at Bnei Brak, and Rabbi Yehoshua’s at Pekiin, yet all of them assembled at Yavneh.[^10]

Rabbi Tarfon was closely attached to his disciple-colleague Rabbi Akiva. In [Ketubot 84b](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.84b), the Gemara is uncertain whether Rabbi Tarfon was Rabbi Akiva’s teacher or colleague. He would say to him: “Akiva, anyone who separates from you is as one who separates from life”: [Kiddushin 66b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.66b), [Zevachim 13a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.13a), Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, chapter 1, at the end of halakhah 1, and Sifrei, Beha’alotekha, section 37. Rabbi Akiva treated him with great respect. In [Bekhorot 4:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bekhorot.4.4), Rabbi Tarfon fed to dogs a cow whose womb had been removed; the Sages ruled that it was kosher. Rabbi Tarfon said: “Your donkey is gone, Tarfon!” Rabbi Akiva replied: “Rabbi Tarfon, you are exempt, for you are an expert recognized by the court…”. In [Menachot 68b](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.68b), Rabbi Tarfon was sitting and struggling with a difficulty. Yehuda ben Nechemiah offered a response, and Rabbi Tarfon fell silent. Yehuda’s face shone with pleasure. Rabbi Akiva said: “Yehuda, does your face shine because you have answered the elder? I wonder whether you will live long.” And so it was.[^11]

The great men of that generation were his disciples. Tosefta Berakhot, chapter 4, describes four elders sitting in Rabbi Yehoshua’s gatehouse—Elazar ben Matya, Chanina ben Chakhinai, Shimon ben Azzai, and Shimon HaTimni—discussing what Rabbi Tarfon had taught them.

Rabbi Oshaya, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaBosem, testified before Rabbi Akiva in Rabbi Tarfon’s name: [Chullin 55b](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.55b). In Tosefta Sheviit 5:8 the reading is “Rabbi Yehuda ben Yeshaya HaBosem.” Rabbi Elazar reports in Rabbi Tarfon’s name in Tosefta Parah, chapter 11.

Rabbi Yehuda was his outstanding disciple from childhood. In [Megillah 20a](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.20a), he says: “I was a child, and I read the Megillah before Rabbi Tarfon.” In [Yevamot 101b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.101b), Rabbi Yehuda says: “Once we were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon…”. In [Nedarim 49b](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.49b), Rabbi Yehuda sits before Rabbi Tarfon, who says: “Your face is bright today.” He replies: “Last night your servants went out…”. In [Shabbat 29b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.29b), Rabbi Yehuda says: “Once we spent Shabbat in the upper room of the house of Nitza in Lod”—where Rabbi Tarfon and the elders were present. In [Bekhorot 45b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.45b), Rabbi Yehuda tells of a man who came before Rabbi Tarfon with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. Rabbi Tarfon said to him: “May there be many like you in Israel!”[^12]

In Jerusalem Talmud, Sotah 2:2, and Tosefta Negaim, chapter 8, Rabbi Yehuda says: “It was Shabbat… I was with Rabbi Tarfon. He said to me: ‘My son, give me my sandal’”—and he learned seven things from him. Rabbi Yehuda also reports his rulings: in [Eruvin 4:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eruvin.4.4), “It happened that Rabbi Tarfon entered unintentionally”; in [Nedarim 6:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Nedarim.6.6), “It happened that Rabbi Tarfon forbade it to me.” Rabbi Yehuda reports in Rabbi Tarfon’s name in [Eruvin 82a](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.82a), [Sukkah 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.31a), and [Niddah 36a](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.36a). He also tells stories about Rabbi Tarfon in Tosefta Sheviit, chapter 4; Shabbat, chapter 6; and Bekhorot, chapter 5.

Rabbi Yossi HaGelili was undoubtedly as old as Rabbi Tarfon, for we find that he was a colleague of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. He had, however, lived in Galilee and only later came before the Sages at Yavneh. Thus [Zevachim 57a](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.57a) recounts that when the question was asked in the vineyard at Yavneh, “For how long may a firstborn offering be eaten?”, Rabbi Tarfon answered. A student who had come before the Sages in the study house for the first time was present; his name was Rabbi Yossi HaGelili. “My master, how do you know this?” he asked. Rabbi Akiva leapt into the discussion, and Rabbi Tarfon withdrew. In Sifrei, Korach, section 42, Rabbi Tarfon calls him “my son.” In Sifrei, Chukkat, Rabbi Tarfon says of the encounter: “I saw the ram butting”—this is Rabbi Akiva; “and behold, a he-goat came from the west”—this is Rabbi Yossi HaGelili.[^13]

Rabbi Shimon reports in Rabbi Tarfon’s name in Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 3:4; Terumot 7:1; and Megillah 1:6. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says: “Once… I came and asked Rabbi Tarfon,” in [Menachot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.31a). His sister’s sons also studied before him: [Zevachim 62b](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.62b).

In [Bekhorot 11a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.11a), we find: “Rabbi Yehuda Nesia had a firstborn donkey, which he sent before Rabbi Tarfon.” This is astonishing: even if one identifies him as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, it cannot be correct. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could not have seen Rabbi Tarfon, for in [Bava Metzia 85a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.85a) he encounters only Rabbi Tarfon’s grandson. *Mevo ha-Mishnah*, page 102, conjectures that the text should read “Rabbi Yehuda, the halakhic instructor of the patriarch’s household”; I too arrived independently at this explanation. Yet this also is incorrect, for Rabbi Yehuda attained that position only after Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel became president at Usha, as explained in his biography. The reading in *Kaftor va-Ferach*, chapter 16, is therefore preferable: it reads only “the patriarch’s household,” referring to the household of Rabban Gamliel. Since Rabbi Tarfon was a priest, they sent it to him. This is the correct explanation.[^14]
**His wealth, generosity, and piety**

Kallah Rabbati, chapter 2, and Vayikra Rabbah 34:16 relate that Rabbi Tarfon was very wealthy but did not give substantial gifts to the poor. Once Rabbi Akiva asked: “Would you like me to acquire a town or two for you?” He agreed and gave Rabbi Akiva four thousand gold dinars. Rabbi Akiva went and distributed them to the poor. When Rabbi Tarfon later met him and asked whether he had purchased the towns, Rabbi Akiva took a book of Psalms and read until he reached the verse: [“He has distributed freely, he has given to the needy” (Psalms 112:9)](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.112.9). This is the same Rabbi Tarfon who says in [Shabbat 25b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.25b): “Who is wealthy? One who has a hundred vineyards, a hundred fields, and a hundred slaves.”[^15]

From that time onward he recognized his error. Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, chapter 4, at the end of halakhah 12, relates that during a famine Rabbi Tarfon devised a means of betrothing three hundred women so that he could feed them terumah. At the end of Avot de-Rabbi Natan, a bride passes Rabbi Tarfon while he is teaching his disciples. He calls for her, brings her into his house, and tells his mother and wife: “Wash her, anoint her, and adorn her, so that she may go to her husband’s house.”

[Nedarim 62a](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.62a) tells that Rabbi Tarfon once ate figs after the drying season was over, when they were ownerless and available to everyone. The owner of the orchard took him for a thief, put him in a sack, and was about to throw him into the river. Rabbi Tarfon cried: “Woe to Tarfon, whom this man is killing!” On hearing this, the man let him go and fled. Rabbi Tarfon grieved all his life that he had made use of the crown of Torah, instead of appeasing the man with money. Kallah, chapter 2, tells the story somewhat differently: Rabbi Tarfon ate dried figs from his own orchard. The tenant farmer did not recognize him and beat him severely. Rabbi Tarfon said nothing until he saw that his life was ebbing away, when he exclaimed: “Woe to you, Tarfon!” The man asked: “Are you Rabbi Tarfon?” “Yes,” he replied. The man tore his hair and cried out. The account in Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit, chapter 4, at the end of halakhah 2, is similar.

Truth was a lamp to his feet, and he was not ashamed to acknowledge it. In Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma, chapter 1, at the end of halakhah 1, he admits to Rabbi Akiva that he had forgotten. In [Beitzah 3:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Beitzah.3.5), when a question was put to him which he could not answer, he entered the study house and asked.

He honored his mother with his own body. [Kiddushin 31b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.31b) relates that whenever his mother wished to climb into bed, he bent down so she could climb upon him; when she wished to get down, she descended upon him.

He was scrupulously careful to avoid sexual impropriety. In [Kiddushin 81b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.81b), he says: “Take care that I am not left alone with my daughter-in-law.” A student who mocked him eventually stumbled into sin with his own mother-in-law.[^16]

His precious aggadic sayings include [Avot 2:15–16](https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.2.15-16): “The day is short, the work is great, the laborers are idle, the reward is abundant, and the master is pressing. It is not your responsibility to finish the work, but neither are you free to desist from it. If you have learned much Torah, they give you much reward; and the master of your work is trustworthy to pay the reward of your labor. Know…”.[^17]

At the end of Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 12, he says that the Holy One, blessed be He, did not cause His presence to dwell upon Israel until they had done work, and that a person dies only through idleness. In [Niddah 13b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.13b), he says of a hand that touches the penis: “Let it be cut off”—it is better for a man’s belly to burst than for him to descend into the pit of destruction. In [Niddah 61a](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.61a), he says: “As for this malicious report, although one ought not to accept it, one ought to take precautions on its account.”

His love for Israel was so great that he says at the end of [Makkot, chapter 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Makkot.1.10): had he been a member of the Sanhedrin when it tried capital cases, no person would ever have been executed. Yet he utterly hated the well-known sectarians. In [Shabbat 116a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.116a), he says: “May I lose my sons if, should their books come into my hands, I do not burn them together with the divine names in them!” Even if someone pursues a person to kill him, or a snake pursues him to bite him, he should enter a place of idol worship rather than their houses, “for these recognize and deny.” Many valuable lessons may be learned from this.[^18]

It was not for nothing that he was described as “a heap of nuts”: [Gittin 67a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.67a) and Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 18. As soon as he opened his mouth, words of wisdom rolled out like precious stones and pearls. Bereshit Rabbah 91:9 records a witty observation by Abba Nehorai: when someone offered a well-formulated teaching before Rabbi Tarfon, he would say “a knob and a flower”; when the teaching was not well formulated, he would say “My son has not gone down with you”—meaning, “my understanding has not accompanied you.”[^19]
**His wife, sons, and daughters**

Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, chapter 4, at the end of halakhah 11, relates that his wife died, and that during the mourning period he said to her sister: “Come in and raise your sister’s children.” He also lived to marry off his son, as in [Kiddushin 81b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.81b). Shimon ben Tarfon is mentioned in [Shevuot 47b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shevuot.47b); perhaps he was his son. We also find that Rabbi Tarfon had a daughter: in [Bava Metzia 85a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.85a), Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi came to Rabbi Tarfon’s town and asked whether that righteous man, who used to speak of losing his sons, had a son. They replied: “He has no son, but he has a daughter’s son.” Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi brought the grandson back to proper conduct, saying: “If you mend your ways, I will give you my daughter.” He did mend his ways. Some say he married her and divorced her; others say he did not marry her at all.

Concerning his death, we find only the account in Eikhah Rabbah, on “The Lord has swallowed up”: some include him among those put to death by the government, while others list Rabbi Elazar Charsanah in his place. We see from this that they themselves were uncertain.

By conjecture, he lived more than seventy years. As explained above, he was about twenty when the Temple was destroyed. We find him still alive after Rabbi Eliezer, and he died approximately fifty-three years after the destruction.[^20]

notes.text: This translation follows the exact published Wikisource witness; it does not certify a new scan proofreading. Obvious transcription slips are translated according to their intelligible sense, with consequential readings noted below. Hyman’s source citations, judgments, and inferences remain attributed to him. Where an edition’s section number has not been matched securely to a modern reference, the old citation is retained without a guessed link.

Hyman cites “Beha’alotekha 37,” a numbering used in his cited edition. The linked Sefaria passage is numbered **Sifrei Bamidbar 75**. Hyman’s proposed revision of the festival list, reported from *Meir Ayin*, remains an attributed emendation, not a silent alteration of the quoted witness. *Hakhel* is the public Torah assembly held after the sabbatical year.

The age calculation and proposed discipleship are Hyman’s historical reconstruction, not explicit dates supplied by the cited passages. The Wikisource witness has ור״י in this calculation, where its context is Rabbi Tarfon. The translation follows that context. “May I lose my sons” renders אקפח את בני, a conventional self-imprecation; it is not a report that he harmed his children.

A daughter’s co-wife can become subject to levirate marriage when the husband dies childless. The schools disagree over whether her relationship to the surviving brother’s daughter exempts her. Hyman quotes Tarfon’s position to discuss his affiliation; this is not a practical ruling.

The Hebrew witness reads אשר גאלני, “who redeemed me,” but the cited Mishnah reads אשר גאלנו, “who redeemed us”; the English gives the matching Mishnah wording. In the robbery case the thief does not know which of the five was robbed. *Terumah* is the priestly portion of produce; second tithe ordinarily has to be eaten in Jerusalem or redeemed.

The source witness has a stray Latin v in the Bava Kamma citation and several spelling slips in this list. The cited passage is **Bava Kamma 2:5**, as Hyman’s earlier list also states. A *mamzer* is a person born of certain prohibited unions; the Kiddushin passage concerns the status of descendants, not erasing the parent’s own status. The Hebrew also gives Yevamot 15:6 for the robbery ruling; it is found in **15:7**, linked in the English. Hyman is listing abbreviated rulings, not supplying their complete conditions.
The Hebrew witness cites **Pesachim 22b**. The matching story is **Pesachim 72b**, which is linked in the English; the Hebrew is preserved unchanged.

This explanation of why Tarfon was not appointed president is Hyman’s conjecture. His rhetoric about not sparing his sons is preserved as his interpretation of the repeated formula, not adopted as a literal biographical fact. The source references in this paragraph are his examples of the expression.
Hyman proposes this as a second explanation, not an established account of the appointment. “Attend to the imperial court” renders לפלוחי לבי קיסר, service or dealings at the emperor’s court.

The Hebrew witness abbreviates the Bnei Brak teacher’s name as ר״י. The translation supplies **Rabbi Akiva** from [Sanhedrin 32b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.32b), which identifies Rabbi Akiva with Bnei Brak, and from the preceding discussion of the academies; this is an editorial expansion, not a changed Hebrew reading. The house-name spellings נחזה and נתזה in this article are rendered consistently as Nitza; no identification of the householder is inferred.

“Your donkey is gone” means that Tarfon thought he must compensate the owner for the cow, even at the cost of his donkey. Rabbi Akiva explains why he is exempt. “And so it was” refers to Akiva’s fear that Yehuda ben Nechemiah would not live long, not to an additional legal conclusion.

The Hebrew abbreviates the man as א״א, meaning “a certain person” here. No personal identity is supplied. Hyman does not reproduce the rest of the conversation after “your servants”; the linked Nedarim passage continues with their eating beets without salt. His later citation **Mishnah Nedarim 6:4** for Yehuda’s report “Tarfon forbade it to me” corresponds to **6:6** in the linked numbering.

The ram and goat are images from Daniel 8. Their application to the encounter is quoted as Tarfon’s characterization in Hyman’s cited Sifrei tradition. The Hebrew witness’s חקת־גג appears to be a damaged section number; no precise modern Sifrei pinpoint is guessed here.

The proposed reading “the patriarch’s household” and its identification with Rabban Gamliel’s household are **Hyman’s textual and historical argument**. The English preserves the distinction between the Bavli’s conventional wording and Hyman’s proposed reading.

These are stories of Tarfon’s earlier conduct and change of heart as Hyman arranges them. Hyman’s closing reference to his definition of wealth is retained; it is not a statement that every wealthy person possessed exactly those holdings.
The quoted request concerns avoiding seclusion with his daughter-in-law, rather than accusing her of wrongdoing. Hyman’s account of the student is retained as the narrative of the cited passage.
Hyman cites **Avot 2:15**, but his quotation continues into **2:16** in the linked numbering. His final “Know…” is an intentional abbreviation of the saying, not an incomplete translation.

*Minim*, rendered “sectarians,” is Hyman’s term in this discussion. The hostile language is translated as historical source content. Hyman does not name a modern community here; the translation adds no such identification.

“A knob and a flower” alludes to the ornamental language of the menorah and expresses approval. “My son has not gone down with you” plays on the words of Genesis 42:38; the parenthetical explanation “my understanding” is Hyman’s own.

Hyman himself marks the lifespan as conjectural and acknowledges uncertainty about the manner of death. The article’s concluding chronology is preserved as his estimate, not promoted to an established date.
